forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Gloucester debt under budget but faces hefty refinancing bill
news_drafts.lead: Gloucester Council's borrowing came in at £262.505m in 2025/26, some £7.5m below the £270m budget, indicating lower spending on long-term assets or better cash management than forecast. However, the council faces a substantial refinancing requirement: 54.47 per cent of its total borrowing is due for repayment or renewal within the next 12 months. This timing challenge arrives as the interest rate outlook has shifted sharply. Commentators had expected further interest rate cuts during 2026, but market sentiment as of early April 2026 now suggests rates will hold steady or rise, driven by inflation and geopolitical risks. The council has protected itself against future rate increases by fixing 100 per cent of its borrowing at set interest rates.

news_drafts.headline: Gloucester City Council receives £15.5m government support to cover budget shortfall
news_drafts.lead: Gloucester City Council has received £15.5m from government in February 2026 to cover a shortfall in its budget after the council identified it could not balance its books. The support was approved conditional on a recovery plan, which has undergone external review and is being monitored internally. Multiple services are forecasting overspends totalling nearly £2m: the parking service (£768k), the commercial property portfolio (£530k), and interest costs (£420k). The council holds no general fund reserves — money set aside as a financial cushion — making tight budgetary control essential. Over 54 per cent of its borrowing comes due within 12 months, creating significant refinancing demands in 2026–27.

news_drafts.headline: Gloucester Council faces £1.7m budget overruns with no financial reserves to absorb them
news_drafts.lead: Gloucester Council is forecast to overspend by more than £1.7m in the current financial year, with no general reserves held to manage unexpected costs. The parking service faces a £768,000 overspend driven by the newly opened Forum car park, which is losing money due to high service charges and low usage. The council's commercial property portfolio is £530,000 over budget as retail tenants leave vacant shops and the council picks up service charges. Interest costs on short-term borrowing are forecast £420,000 over budget in a volatile rate environment. The council explicitly states it "does not have any general fund reserves to deal with unplanned variances" and relies on accurate forecasting and tight budgetary control. This comes after the council received £15.5m in exceptional financial support from central government in February following an application for emergency help.

findings.headline: Investment returns maintained at 3.25% (short-term) and 3.80% (CCLA) despite Bank Rate falling 0.75%.
findings.detail: Despite three successive 0.25% Bank Rate cuts during 2025/26, the council maintained competitive investment returns. Short-term balances averaged £14.148m during the year (ending at £4.290m), with £5.919m in longer-term CCLA funds. This demonstrates effective cash positioning.
findings.matters: Investment performance that holds up despite declining interest rates indicates effective treasury management and good cash positioning, supporting confidence in the council's financial stewardship.
findings.figures: Short-term return: 3.25%; CCLA return: 3.80%; Average short-term balance: £14.148m; Bank Rate fell three times by 0.25% each
findings.quote: Investment returns remained robust throughout 2025/26 despite Bank Rate reducing steadily through the course of the financial year (three 0.25% rate cuts in total).

findings.headline: Interest rate outlook shifted from expected cuts to rate holds or increases due to inflation and geopolitical risks.
findings.detail: Bank Rate fell 0.75% in three cuts during 2025/26 (May, August, December from 4.50% to 3.75%). However, as of early April 2026, market sentiment has shifted. Commentators now expect no further rate cuts for some time and anticipate rates may increase to counteract inflation driven by Middle East-related energy cost pressures.
findings.matters: The council's plan to refinance the Forum's short-term borrowing into long-term debt now faces a worse rate environment than was expected at the start of the year. This will increase the long-term cost of funding the capital project.
findings.figures: Bank Rate fell from 4.50% to 3.75% in 2025/26. PWLB 1-year rates ranged 4.25%–5.28%; 10-year rates ranged 5.13%–5.88%
findings.quote: As of early April 2026, market sentiment has been heavily influenced by the Middle East conflict. Commentators anticipate a growing risk of inflation, meaning interest rates will not be cut for some time, and may increase to counteract inflationary pressures arising from steepening energy costs.

findings.headline: Forum capital project is being funded with short-term borrowing; long-term refinancing will occur when construction completes.
findings.detail: The council deliberately chose to borrow short-term rather than long-term for the Forum capital project, taking advantage of short-term rates being lower than long-term rates on the yield curve. The council plans to absorb these financing costs now and spread them over the asset's life. Long-term refinancing will occur after construction completes.
findings.matters: This creates a timing risk: the council will need to refinance into long-term debt when the Forum completes, at whatever interest rates exist at that time. If rates rise before refinancing, the long-term cost of funding the capital project will be materially higher.
findings.figures: No new long-term borrowing undertaken in 2025/26; short-term rates lower than long-term rates; PWLB 10-year rates averaged 5.38% (range 5.13%–5.88%)
findings.quote: As the Forum is still under construction we are able to absorb these financing costs and spread them over the life of the asset. Once the asset is complete we will make a decision, alongside our advisors, on the best way to structure our borrowing.

findings.headline: All net debt is fixed rate; no variable rate exposure
findings.detail: The council has structured 100% of its net debt at fixed interest rates and holds zero variable rate debt. This protects it against future interest rate rises on its existing borrowing.
findings.matters: This shows how the council is managing interest rate risk and means debt service costs are locked in regardless of future rate movements.
findings.quote: Upper limit of fixed interest based on net debt 0% - 100% 100%

findings.headline: 54.47% of external debt matures within 12 months, creating substantial refinancing requirement
findings.detail: More than half of Gloucester's total debt stock is due to mature or be refinanced within one year. This concentration in short-term maturities means the council must access debt markets to replace or repay these loans.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand refinancing risk and whether the council can secure replacement funding; market conditions or availability could affect the council's position.
